subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 6 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy. Be a Musician. But do not be fooled by the musical title: the real computing idea in this unit is repetition — teaching the computer to do something again and again. Music is simply the fun, natural way to meet that idea, because music is full of repeating beats and repeating choruses. The computing word for repetition is iteration — repeating the same block of code over and over. Learning when to use each loop is the heart of the unit. You meet three ways to repeat in Scratch: the forever loop, which never stops; the repeat ( ) loop, which repeats a set number of times and then stops; and the repeat until ( ) loop, which keeps going until something becomes true, such as a key being pressed. They predict the outcome of an algorithm before running it — reading the steps to work out what they will hear. And they compare and contrast two algorithms written for the same task, deciding which is better suited (if you want a beat exactly three times and then stop, is forever or repeat (3) the right tool?).
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 4 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Explain that repetition (the computing word is iteration) means doing something again and again.
Tell the difference between the three loops: forever, repeat ( ) and repeat until ( ).
Explain count-controlled repetition (a set number of times) and condition-controlled repetition (until something becomes true).
Predict the outcome of an algorithm that contains repetition, then check it by running the program.
Compare and contrast two algorithms written for the same task and say which one is best suited.
Develop a program with iteration in Scratch, using a loop to make sound.
Use the volume blocks set volume to ( ) % and change volume by ( ), including a negative change to get quieter.
Add the free Music extension and compose a short rhythm or tune with play drum and play note, and add a comment to explain the code.

Before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already follow and correct an algorithm that uses iteration, build a program with the repeat command (met in Unit 4), and add comments to code. A quick recap of repeat at the start of Session 2 is usually enough.

concepts.title: Repetition all around us (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: Repetition means doing something again and again. It is everywhere — in songs, in games, and in everyday jobs. The computing word for repetition is iteration. When we tell a computer to repeat a block of instructions, we use a loop. dum, tak, tak. We just repeated the same beat. Repeating like that is called repetition.
concepts.example: Repetition is what makes music feel like music. Start with music, because they can hear it.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you continue a simple pattern? Can you give one everyday example of repeating until a job is done? Can you point to the part of a song or chant that repeats, and count how many times?

concepts.title: Meet the loops: forever and repeat
concepts.explanation: In Scratch, a loop repeats the blocks placed inside it. Today we meet two. The forever loop repeats and never stops — the code inside runs round and round until you press the red Stop. Add a drum-style sprite with the Add Sprite button, then find forever and repeat ( ) in the orange Control blocks. Build this tiny program together and run it with the green flag Open Scratch and click Create on the projector.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: meet the loops: forever and repeat. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you run and stop a forever loop? Can you drag a loop block and put a sound block inside it?

concepts.title: Read it, predict it: algorithms and volume
concepts.explanation: An algorithm is a set of steps in the right order. Before we run a program, a good musician-programmer predicts what it will do — reads the steps and works out what they will hear. Try it: build it in Scratch to check the prediction. Check yourself: Can you work out how many times a loop runs? Can you understand that a negative change makes the volume smaller, and that set and change are different? Do you predict before running, rather than running first and guessing after?
concepts.example: Today we also meet the volume blocks: set volume to ( ) % fixes the loudness, and change volume by ( ) adds to it. A negative number, like -10, makes it quieter.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you work out how many times a loop runs? Can you understand that a negative change makes the volume smaller, and that set and change are different? Do you predict before running, rather than running first and guessing after?

concepts.title: Repeat until: a rhythm that stops on a key
concepts.explanation: The third loop is repeat until ( ) — the condition-controlled loop. It keeps repeating while the condition is false and stops the moment the condition becomes true. We give it a condition to watch using a Sensing block, key ( ) pressed?. This is the classic drum program from the textbook. First act it out: “Tap the desk. keep tapping. STOP when I raise my hand.” The raised hand is the condition. You repeated the tap until my hand went up — Scratch can do that too.
concepts.example: Find one real example of repeat until: a rhythm that stops on a key around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drop a key ( ) pressed? condition into a repeat until loop?

concepts.title: Be a musician: compose and compare
concepts.explanation:
We switch on the free Music extension and use loops to build an original rhythm and a short tune. We also practise the syllabus skill of comparing two algorithms written for the same task, and we add a comment to explain our code.

In Scratch, click the Add Extension button (bottom-left) and choose Music. New green blocks appear, including set tempo to ( ), play drum ( ) for ( ) beats and play note ( ) for ( ) beats. In play drum, 1 is the Snare Drum (a sharp “tak” ) and 2 is the Bass Drum (a deep “dum” ). In play note, 60 is a nice middle note; bigger is higher, smaller is lower.
concepts.example: The beats number is how long the sound lasts — the very idea from Session 1: 0.5 is a short note, 1 a one-beat note, 2 a long note. Build a simple hand-drum rhythm together, wrapped in a repeat loop so it plays four times
concepts.checkYourself: Can you build a rhythm inside a loop and change the tempo? Can you compare two algorithms and say which suits the task? Can you add a sensible comment? Can you add the Music extension?

I can tell the difference between the three loops: forever, repeat ( ) and repeat until ( ).
I can explain count-controlled repetition (a set number of times) and condition-controlled repetition (until something becomes true).
I can predict the outcome of an algorithm that contains repetition, then check it by running the program.
I can compare and contrast two algorithms written for the same task and say which one is best suited.
I can develop a program with iteration in Scratch, using a loop to make sound.
I can use the volume blocks set volume to ( ) % and change volume by ( ), including a negative change to get quieter.
I can add the free Music extension and compose a short rhythm or tune with play drum and play note, and add a comment to explain the code.
